exam: A 6‑month‑old infant presents with polyuria, failure to thrive and hypokalaemia. Which tubular defect is most likely? — NKCC2 (Type I) defect in the thick ascending limb.
How does indomethacin improve electrolyte balance in Bartter syndrome? — It inhibits renal prostaglandin E2, decreasing renin release and reducing salt loss.
What key feature distinguishes Bartter from Gitelman syndrome? — Early onset with hypercalciuria in Bartter versus hypomagnesaemia and later presentation in Gitelman.
A patient on chronic loop diuretics shows similar labs to Bartter. What question clarifies the diagnosis? — Ask about diuretic use or obtain a drug history; discontinue diuretics and reassess.
What is the most dangerous acute complication of untreated Bartter syndrome? — Cardiac arrhythmia from severe hypokalaemia.
Why is spironolactone added after NSAIDs in management? — It provides additional potassium‑sparing effect while NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin‑driven loss.
In a low‑resource setting without genetic testing, which investigations are essential? — Serum electrolytes, urine calcium/creatinine ratio, blood pressure, and renal ultrasound if possible.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate hospital admission? — New onset palpitations or syncope suggesting arrhythmia.
ai.title: Bartter Syndrome
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A rare inherited renal tubular disorder causing salt wasting, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and hypercalciuria. Presents with growth failure, polyuria and nephrocalcinosis, especially in low‑resource settings where diagnosis is clinical.

b: Diagnosis requires persistent hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, normal or low blood pressure, and hypercalciuria.
Exclude diuretic use, vomiting, or gastrointestinal loss.
sections.p: Bartter syndrome is a group of autosomal recessive defects of the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle that impair Na⁺‑K⁺‑2Cl⁻ (NKCC2) or related channels, leading to renal salt loss, secondary hyperreninaemia and metabolic alkalosis.

b: Mild: stable electrolytes, normal growth.
Moderate: growth retardation, polyuria, intermittent hypokalaemia.
Severe: failure to thrive, nephrocalcinosis, chronic kidney disease.
sections.p: Severity is gauged by growth parameters, electrolyte derangement, and renal complications.

b: Type I (SLC12A1) – NKCC2 defect – most severe, early onset.
Type II (KCNJ1) – ROMK channel defect – early infancy.
Type III (CLCNKB) – ClC‑KB chloride channel – later presentation.
Type IV (BSND, CLCNKA/B) – combined defect with sensorineural deafness.
Secondary mimics: chronic diuretic abuse, laxative use, severe vomiting.
sections.p: Genetic mutations affecting TAL transport are the primary cause; in low‑resource settings consider secondary causes that mimic the picture.

b: Polyuria >2 L/m²/day.
Persistent hypokalaemia (<3.5 mmol/L).
Metabolic alkalosis (pH > 7.45, HCO₃⁻ > 30 mmol/L).
Hypercalciuria (>0.2 mmol/kg/day).
sections.p: Children present with polyuria, polydipsia, growth failure and sometimes developmental delay. Physical exam may reveal dehydration, low BMI and, in advanced disease, palpable kidneys from nephrocalcinosis.

t.b: Confirms hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, normal sodium; guides replacement.
Detects hypercalciuria; if unavailable, use spot urine calcium.
Looks for nephrocalcinosis; if ultrasound not available, rely on clinical suspicion.
Identifies specific mutation; not essential for acute management.
Shows normal or low BP, distinguishing from hyperaldosteronism.

b: Sudden weakness or palpitations → possible ventricular arrhythmia.
Rapid weight loss or oliguria → acute kidney injury.
Persistent hypercalciuria → nephrolithiasis or renal failure.
sections.p: Uncontrolled electrolyte loss can precipitate cardiac arrhythmias, severe dehydration, and progressive renal impairment.

b: Potassium‑sparing supplementation (oral KCl) to keep K⁺ > 3.5 mmol/L.
Indomethacin or other NSAIDs to lower prostaglandin‑mediated salt loss; avoid in active infection or peptic ulcer disease.
Spironolactone or eplerenone for additional potassium retention; avoid if hyperkalaemia risk.
Adequate hydration and low‑salt diet to limit polyuria.
Monitor growth, renal ultrasound and serum electrolytes every 3‑6 months.
sections.p: Treat the underlying tubular defect with electrolyte replacement and drugs that reduce renal prostaglandin production, while monitoring growth and renal function.

b: Quarterly serum K⁺, Na⁺, bicarbonate, creatinine.
Annual renal ultrasound.
Counselling families about genetic inheritance and need for sibling screening.
sections.p: Regular outpatient review focuses on growth, electrolyte balance, and renal imaging. Early detection of nephrocalcinosis allows dietary calcium moderation.

b: Gitelman syndrome – distal tubule defect, presents later with hypomagnesaemia.
Vomiting or nasogastric suction – loss of gastric acid, not renal.
Loop diuretic abuse – similar labs but history of medication use.
sections.p: Other causes of hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

b: Serum calcium may be normal even with high urinary loss.
Blood pressure can be low, masking volume depletion.
Urine sodium may be low if patient is dehydrated, hiding renal salt wasting.
sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite disease activity.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe weakness, palpitations or syncope (possible arrhythmia).
Rapid decline in urine output or rising creatinine.
Persistent vomiting or inability to maintain oral intake.
